claims.source: The frequency of the oscillatory fluctuation within a cluster was not strictly fixed at a constant value.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the variability in oscillation frequency.

claims.claim: Spontaneous behaviors such as whisking, twitching, or struggling could cause functional hyperemia resulting in interruption of periodic oscillations.
claims.source: It is possible that spontaneous vasomotion detected in our system through the intact skull in awake in vivo mice was less periodic because spontaneous behaviors such as whisking, twitching, or struggling could cause functional hyperemia resulting in the interruption of apparent periodic oscillations.
claims.evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation for the observed variability.

claims.claim: Horizontally oscillating visual stimuli induce involuntary eye movement where the line of sight follows the stimuli in head-fixed mice.
claims.source: Horizontally oscillating visual stimuli are known to induce involuntary eye movement and the line of sight follows the stimuli in head-fixed mice.
claims.evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Repeated presentation of HOKR stimuli induces a gradual increase in the amplitude of eye movement.
claims.source: Repeated presentation of the stimuli also induces a gradual increase in the amplitude of the eye movement and the small flocculus region of the cerebellum has been shown to be responsible for this learning (Aziz et al., 2014; Ito, 1982).
claims.evidence: The Results section cites sources supporting this learning phenomenon.

claims.claim: In Novice mice, TexasRed signals fluctuated with non-fixed low frequencies consisting mainly of <0.3 Hz.
claims.source: In response to the first visual training session, fixed frequency oscillation of the TexasRed intensity at the primary visual cortex (V1) was not observed. TexasRed signals in these 'Novice' mice, fluctuated with non-fixed low frequencies which consisted mainly of <0.3 Hz (Figure 3C, left).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In Trained mice, Fourier transform of TexasRed signal at V1 revealed a clear sharp peak at 0.25 Hz.
claims.source: After a couple of more training sessions and just before the fourth training session, TexasRed was administered again. In these 'Trained' mice, the TexasRed signal in the cortex fluctuated periodically. Fourier transform of the TexasRed signal at V1 during the 15 min training session revealed a clear sharp peak in the amplitude spectrum at 0.25 Hz, which was not observed in the Novice mice (Figure 3C, middle).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Second and third harmonic signals were sometimes observed in the frequency spectrum.
claims.source: We also noticed that, although the amplitudes were often much smaller, second and third harmonic signals were sometimes observed.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claims.claim: Second harmonic signal could be explained if visually induced vasomotion reacts to both directions of oscillating stimuli.
claims.source: The second harmonic signal could be explained if visually induced vasomotion reacts to both directions of oscillating stimuli.
claims.evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claims.claim: In Expert mice, the 0.25 Hz fluctuation in TexasRed signal becomes visible in raw traces.
claims.source: With further repeated training sessions (8–11 training sessions), the TexasRed signal fluctuation further becomes more strongly tuned to the frequency of the visual stimuli ('Expert', Figure 3C, right). In this Expert mouse, the 0.25 Hz fluctuation in the TexasRed signal becomes visible even in the raw traces.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In Expert mice, as soon as visual stimulus started, a sharp rise in 0.25 Hz frequency amplitude increased.
claims.source: Before the visual stimulus, the amplitude at 0.25 Hz was negligible; however, as soon as the visual stimulus started, a sharp rise in 0.25 Hz frequency amplitude increased.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the temporal dynamics in Expert mice.

claims.claim: Vasomotion amplitude locked to visual stimulus frequency quickly dissipated upon cessation of visual stimulus.
claims.source: The amplitude gradually declined but stayed significant until the cessation of the visual stimulus and the vasomotion amplitude locked to the visual stimulus frequency quickly dissipated (Figure 3D and E, left panel).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: Averaged PR0.25 in the whole brain surface ROI gradually increased as training progressed.
claims.source: Averaged PR0.25 in the whole brain surface ROI gradually increased as the training progressed (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: PR0.25 in V1 and V2 was high but not particularly high compared to S1 or Cb or anywhere else that could be observed.
claims.source: The location of V1, secondary visual cortex (V2), primary sensory cortex (S1), and the cerebellum (Cb) was roughly identified based on the coordinates of the mouse brain atlas by referring to the bregma and lambda locations. PR0.25 in V1 and V2 was high but not particularly high compared to S1 or Cb or, in fact, anywhere else that could be observed.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the spatial distribution of PR0.25.

claims.claim: The phase of 0.25 Hz signal fluctuation was nearly synchronized across different ROIs.
claims.source: An example of the actual TexasRed signal fluctuation trace in various ROI is shown in Figure 3I. The 0.25 Hz signal fluctuations were apparent in all ROI and, in addition, the phase of the signal fluctuation was also nearly synchronized (n = 5 animals; data not shown).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Frequency and phase-locked vasomotion are not restricted to the visual-related area.
claims.source: These data show that frequency and phase-locked vasomotion are not restricted to the visual-related area, and enhancement and entrainment of vasomotion are observed widely throughout the surface of the brain.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the spatial distribution data.

claims.claim: If TexasRed had to be injected before every training session, the mouse did not learn HOKR very well.
claims.source: However, we found that, if TexasRed had to be injected before every training session, the mouse did not learn very well.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claims.claim: Stress induced by tail vein injection may interfere with the HOKR learning process.
claims.source: It is possible that the stress induced by the tail vein injection interfered with the learning process.
claims.evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claims.claim: Already acquired HOKR learning with multiple training sessions does not get lost with stressful injection.
claims.source: However, as demonstrated below, an already acquired HOKR learning with multiple training sessions does not get lost with the stressful injection.
claims.evidence: The Results section states this observation.

claims.claim: Blood vessels appear as dark 'shadows' in the dYFP fluorescence image.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A, the blood vessels are devoid of the fluorescence from the YFP expressed in astrocytes, and thus the blood vessels appear as dark regions in the images.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Dilation or constriction would appear as a decrease and increase in the fluorescence signal of YFP.
claims.source: Therefore, dilation or constriction would appear as a decrease and increase in the fluorescence signal of the YFP.
claims.evidence: The Results section infers this from the shadow imaging principle.

claims.claim: Both TexasRed and dYFP signals fluctuated with 0.25 Hz temporal frequency directly matching the visual stimulus, but mirrored in direction of change.
claims.source: Both TexasRed and dYFP signals simultaneously monitored with fiber photometry fluctuated with the 0.25 Hz temporal frequency directly matching the visual stimulus, but mirrored in the direction of change (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Not only in the cortex but also deep in the cerebellum, vasomotion can be induced with visual stimulation.
claims.source: The TexasRed signal oscillations were locked to the temporal frequency of the visual stimulus. This shows that, not only in the cortex but also deep in the cerebellum, vasomotion can be induced with visual stimulation.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the fiber photometry data.

claims.claim: The average phase shift of dYFP relative to TexasRed was 184.4° ± 17.6°.
claims.source: The average phase shift of dYFP relative to TexasRed was 184.4° ± 17.6° (S.D.) (Figure 4G; n = 13 segments with 5 min durations each), indicating that these signals were nearly completely inverted.
claims.evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: dYFP signals can be used for assessing vasomotion dynamics.
claims.source: This shows that dYFP signals can be used for assessing the vasomotion dynamics.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the phase analysis.

claims.claim: Robust HOKR learning could not be reliably induced in Mlc1-tTA::tetO-YCnano50 transgenic mice for unknown reasons.
claims.source: Unfortunately, robust HOKR learning could not be reliably induced in this line of transgenic mice for unknown reasons.
claims.evidence: The Results section states this observation.

claims.claim: When signals collected using 400 µm diameter fiber photometry were analyzed, TexasRed fluorescence and autofluorescence did not mirror completely and a significant shift in phase was observed (246.9° ± 49.9°).
claims.source: However, when the signals collected using the 400 µm diameter fiber photometry were analyzed, TexasRed fluorescence and autofluorescence did not mirror completely and a significant shift in the phase was observed (Figure 4H–J; 246.9° ± 49.9° [S.D.], n = 28 segments).
claims.evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data shown in Figure 4H-J.

claims.claim: The phase shift in autofluorescence could be due to the additive effect of 'shadow' imaging and concentration fluctuation of autofluorescent metabolite.
claims.source: The phase shift in the autofluorescence could be due to the additive effect of 'shadow' imaging of the vessel and to the concentration fluctuation of the autofluorescent metabolite.
claims.evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claims.claim: The amplitude of 0.25 Hz temporal frequency component of both TexasRed and autofluorescence signals increased with training.
claims.source: The TexasRed fluorescence and the autofluorescence signals are shown for the initial sessions (Novice, Figure 4K) and after several training sessions (Trained). The amplitude of the 0.25 Hz temporal frequency component of both the TexasRed and the autofluorescence signals increased with training (Figure 4K and L).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4K and L.

claims.claim: A strong correlation between PR0.25 of autofluorescence and that of TexasRed was found.
claims.source: PR0.25 of autofluorescence was plotted against that of the TexasRed for multiple training sessions and a strong correlation between these two parameters was found (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the correlation shown in Figure 4M.

claims.claim: PR0.25 of autofluorescence reflects the amplitude of vasomotion locked to the visual stimulation cycle.
claims.source: Therefore, although the autofluorescence dynamics result from the fluctuations reflecting the 'shadow' of vasomotion and an unknown fluctuation source, the PR0.25 apparently reflects the amplitude of the vasomotion locked to the visual stimulation cycle.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the correlation data.

claims.claim: Autofluorescence fluctuations followed changes in temporal frequency of visual stimulation from 0.15 Hz to 0.50 Hz.
claims.source: First, the temporal frequency was changed from 0.25 Hz to 0.15 Hz or 0.50 Hz while keeping other parameters fixed. Interestingly, the autofluorescence fluctuations followed the changes in the temporal frequency, and a clear sharp amplitude at the frequency locked to the presented visual stimulation was evident in the amplitude spectrum in all conditions (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: No significant difference in peak ratio was found for temporal frequencies ranging from 0.15 to 0.50 Hz.
claims.source: The peak ratio of the autofluorescence was examined for temporal frequency ranging from 0.15 to 0.50 Hz and normalized to that of 0.25 Hz (PR0.25; Figure 5D, left panel). No significant difference was found, showing that vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined (0.15-0.50 Hz).
claims.source: No significant difference was found, showing that vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Visually induced vasomotion quickly adapted to any new frequency tested and the reversibility of adaptation was confirmed.
claims.source: The visually induced vasomotion quickly adapted to any new frequency tested and the reversibility of the adaptation was confirmed.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claims.claim: Temporal frequency-locked vasomotion was apparent in low 4° amplitude as well as in high 25° amplitude.
claims.source: Similarly, the effect of changing the spatial amplitude of the horizontal oscillations was examined, while keeping other parameters fixed. A large amplitude would require the mouse to move its eyes largely within their eye sockets. The temporal frequency-locked vasomotion was apparent in the low 4° amplitude as well as in the high 25° amplitude (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Vasomotion was substantially induced in response to any amplitude between 4° and 25°.
claims.source: The relative peak ratio normalized to that of 17° amplitude showed that the vasomotion was substantially induced in response to any amplitude between 4° and 25° (Figure 5D, middle panel).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Vasomotion could follow visual stimuli irrespective of the fineness of the presented stripes.
claims.source: Lastly, the horizontal spatial cycle of the vertical stripes was varied (Figure 5C). Again, the vasomotion could follow the visual stimuli irrespective of the fineness of the presented stripes (Figure 5D, right panel).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: The eye tracked visual stimulation well with virtually no phase shift relative to the visual stimulation cycle.
claims.source: First, the right eye trace in response to the horizontally oscillating visual stimulus was examined (Figure 6A). The eye tracked the visual stimulation well and there was virtually no phase shift in the eye trace relative to the visual stimulation cycle (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: The phase of TexasRed signal in the flocculus was either 0° or 180° relative to visual stimulation, depending on the animal.
claims.source: The TexasRed signal fluctuation in the flocculus in the right hemisphere was oscillatory with the visual stimulation; however, the phase of the TexasRed signal was either 0° or 180° relative to the visual stimulation, depending on the animal (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Maximum vasodilation and vasoconstriction occur when the speed of eye movement reaches zero.
claims.source: In either mouse, the maximum vasodilation and vasoconstriction occur when the speed of the eye movement reaches zero.
claims.evidence: The Results section infers this from the phase relationship.

claims.claim: Under anesthesia with isoflurane, eye movement was not induced and dYFP signal did not oscillate.
claims.source: To address this possibility, the mouse was anesthetized by isoflurane (Figure 6D). Under anesthesia, the eye fails to follow the screen. The vasomotion was detected with the 'shadow' imaging method by studying the dYFP fluctuations. No oscillatory signals were detected in the dYFP.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Visual stimulus on the presented screen does not reach the optical fiber to directly induce oscillatory signals.
claims.source: Next, in the TexasRed injected mouse, the HOKR visual stimulation was presented, which induced a nice eye movement following the visual stimulus (Figure 6E). However, in this case, we did not send the excitation light through the optical fiber but kept the PMT active. If the visual stimulus on the presented screen is somehow reaching the optical fiber, then it should be detected in this condition, but it was not.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes control experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of vasomotion, respectively.
claims.source: The amplitude of the oscillatory eye movement was plotted against the PR0.25 of the TexasRed during a single visual session (Figure 6G). The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of the vasomotion, respectively, and no correlation was found.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: No correlation was found between eye movement amplitude and PR0.25 of TexasRed.
claims.source: The amplitude of the oscillatory eye movement was plotted against the PR0.25 of the TexasRed during a single visual session (Figure 6G). The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of the vasomotion, respectively, and no correlation was found.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Repeated HOKR training results in larger amplitude of eye oscillations, reaching close to the actual visual presentation amplitude.
claims.source: Repeated HOKR training usually results in a larger amplitude of the eye oscillations, which reaches close to the actual visual presentation amplitude.
claims.evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge.

claims.claim: HOKR performance increase relies on neuronal and glial activity in the cerebellar flocculus.
claims.source: It has been shown that HOKR performance increase relies on the neuronal and glial activity in the cerebellar flocculus (Kanaya et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The Results section cites a source supporting this mechanism.

claims.claim: HOKR performance increased with repeated training sessions during day 1.
claims.source: As described previously, HOKR performance increased with repeated training sessions during day 1 (Figure 7B-D).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: PR0.25 of autofluorescence signal changes with spaced training protocol basically followed plastic changes of eye movement.
claims.source: The PR0.25 of the autofluorescence signal changes with the spaced training protocol basically followed the plastic changes of the eye movement (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: A strong correlation was found between average HOKR relative gains and average PR0.25 values across 10 tests.
claims.source: The average HOKR relative gains were plotted against the average PR0.25 values and a strong correlation was found (Figure 7F; each data point represents an average score of n = 15 mice and 10 data points are shown for the 10 tests).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: A large variance was found both in HOKR relative gain and PR0.25 of autofluorescence fluctuations across animals.
claims.source: In addition, it should be pointed out that a large variance was found both in the HOKR relative gain and the PR0.25 of the autofluorescence fluctuations across animals (X and Y error bars indicate S.D. in Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the variance shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: A moderate but significant correlation was found between HOKR relative gain on day 5 normalized to fourth training on day 1 and PR0.25 of autofluorescence fluctuations during last 5 min of fourth training session on day 1.
claims.source: HOKR relative gain on day 5 normalized to that for the fourth training on day 1 was plotted against the PR0.25 of the autofluorescence fluctuations during the last 5 min of the fourth training session on day 1 (Figure 7G). Interestingly, a moderate but significant correlation between these parameters was found (n = 15 mice).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: The level of visually induced vasomotion may contribute to the consolidation of HOKR performance in later days.
claims.source: This may suggest that the level of visually induced vasomotion contributes to the consolidation of HOKR performance in later days.
claims.evidence: The Results section proposes this interpretation of the correlation.

claims.claim: There is a complex and intimate relationship between vasomotion and neuronal circuit plasticity, learning, and memory.
claims.source: These results imply a complex and intimate relationship between vasomotion and neuronal circuit plasticity, learning, and memory.
claims.evidence: The Results section concludes this from the correlation findings.

claims.claim: The initial drive for vasomotion or sensory-evoked hyperemia must be coming from neuronal activity in the visual system.
claims.source: The initial drive for the vasomotion, or the sensory-evoked hyperemia, must be coming from the neuronal activity in the visual system.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this mechanism.

claims.claim: Visually induced vasomotion is likely triggered by activation of neurovascular interaction.
claims.source: The visually induced vasomotion is likely triggered by activation of the neurovascular interaction (Kayser et al., 2004; van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claims.claim: The global entrainment could be realized through separate mechanisms from local neurovascular coupling.
claims.source: The global entrainment could be realized through separate mechanisms from the local neurovascular coupling.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claims.claim: Repeated visual stimulus may induce synaptic plasticity at neuronal projections from retina to a central nucleus that controls brain-wide vasomotion, such as in the autonomic nerve system.
claims.source: Repeated visual stimulus may induce synaptic plasticity not in the visual system but at the neuronal projections from the retina to a central nucleus that controls a brain-wide vasomotion, such as in the autonomic nerve system (Korte et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this mechanism with citation.

claims.claim: Neurovascular coupling could be enhanced with increased responsiveness of vascules and vascular-to-vascular coupling could also be potentiated.
claims.source: Instead, the neurovascular coupling could be enhanced with increased responsiveness of the vascules and vascular-to-vascular coupling could also be potentiated.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this alternative mechanism.

claims.claim: Glucose and oxygen are likely to be abundantly delivered during vasodilation phase compared to vasoconstriction phase of vasomotion.
claims.source: Glucose and oxygen are likely to be abundantly delivered during the vasodilation phase compared to the vasoconstriction phase of vasomotion.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this based on physiological reasoning.

claims.claim: Concentration fluctuation of metabolites such as NADH, NADPH, and FAD could lag in time to changes in blood flow.
claims.source: These molecules will trigger cell metabolism and endogenous fluorescent molecules such as NADH, NADPH, and FAD may increase or decrease with a certain delay. These molecules are required for biochemical reactions to occur. Therefore, the concentration fluctuation of these metabolites could lag in time to the changes in the blood flow.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this explanation for the phase shift.

claims.claim: Stress induced by tail-vein injection could not interfere with the generation of visually induced vasomotion.
claims.source: Before session 4, TexasRed was injected again to visualize the vasomotion. The oscillatory vasomotion was clearly observed in session 4, indicating that the stress induced by tail-vein injection could not interfere with the generation of visually induced vasomotion.
claims.evidence: The Discussion concludes this from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: It is not possible to distinguish whether visually induced oscillatory vasomotion was driven by mechanisms of spontaneous vasomotion or functional hyperemia.
claims.source: It is not possible to distinguish whether the visually induced oscillatory vasomotion observed in this study was driven by the mechanisms of spontaneous vasomotion or functional hyperemia.
claims.evidence: The Discussion acknowledges this limitation.

claims.claim: Spontaneous vasomotion requires coordinated activity of vascular SMCs.
claims.source: The spontaneous vasomotion requires the coordinated activity of the vascular SMCs.
claims.evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Oscillatory release of calcium ions from sarcoplasmic reticulum results in oscillations in membrane potential of SMCs.
claims.source: Oscillatory release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum results in oscillations in the membrane potential of SMCs. Via the gap junctions between SMCs, synchronized oscillations are created (Haddock et al., 2006; Haddock and Hill, 2002; Hill et al., 1999; Peng et al., 2001; Schuster et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claims.claim: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by SMCs in precapillary arterioles.
claims.source: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by the SMCs in precapillary arterioles; however, capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes (Peppiatt et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this knowledge.

claims.claim: Capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes.
claims.source: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by the SMCs in precapillary arterioles; however, capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes (Peppiatt et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claims.claim: Whether astrocytic calcium is involved in controlling local cerebral blood flow is in question.
claims.source: Astrocytes also constitute the neurovascular unit; however, whether astrocytic calcium is involved in controlling local cerebral blood flow is in question (Ozawa et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source questioning this mechanism.

claims.claim: Astrocytes could regulate vasomotor amplitudes via stretch-mediated feedback.
claims.source: It is still possible that astrocytes could regulate vasomotor amplitudes via stretch-mediated feedback (Bazargani and Attwell, 2016; Haidey et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this possibility.

claims.claim: Spontaneous vasomotion has been suggested to be driven by periodic neural activity in the resting state.
claims.source: Spontaneous vasomotion has been suggested to be driven by the periodic neural activity in the resting state (Martuzzi et al., 2009; Mateo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claims.claim: Neuronal projections from neuronal nuclei projecting to the whole brain may be controlling and synchronizing vasomotion via neurovascular coupling.
claims.source: Neuronal projections from the neuronal nuclei projecting to the whole brain may be controlling and synchronizing vasomotion via neurovascular coupling (Korte et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this possibility.

claims.claim: Ultra-slow vasomotion could be driven not only by neuronal rhythms but also by oscillatory systemic changes, such as blood pressure and carbon dioxide in the blood.
claims.source: It is also possible that ultra-slow vasomotion could be driven not only by the neuronal rhythms but also by the oscillatory systemic changes, such as blood pressure and carbon dioxide in the blood (Panerai et al., 1998; Sassaroli et al., 2012; Wise et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this possibility.

claims.claim: Functional hyperemia has been shown to be induced by visual stimulation.
claims.source: Functional hyperemia has been shown to be induced by visual stimulation (Heeger et al., 2000; Kayser et al., 2004; Niessing et al., 2005; Rivadulla et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2021; Stickland et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this phenomenon.

claims.claim: If a pulsatile visual stimulus is periodically presented, that would result in vasomotion fluctuation with the same frequency as the presented visual stimulus.
claims.source: If a pulsatile visual stimulus is periodically presented, that would result in vasomotion fluctuation with the same frequency as the presented visual stimulus (Kayser et al., 2004; van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this relationship.

claims.claim: Previously, visual stimulus-evoked vasomotion was reported to be restricted to the visual cortex.
claims.source: Previously, such visual stimulus-evoked vasomotion was reported to be restricted to the visual cortex (van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source reporting this finding.

claims.claim: Vasomotion entrainment may be induced in other areas as well, including the limbic system and the brain stem.
claims.source: It is possible that vasomotion entrainment is induced in other areas as well, including the limbic system and the brain stem.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claims.claim: Mathematical modeling has shown that effective vascular resistance decreases with vasomotion.
claims.source: Mathematical modeling has shown that effective vascular resistance decreases with vasomotion (Meyer et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claims.claim: Low-frequency vasomotion has been shown to be beneficial for tissue oxygenation, especially in regions where perfusion is restricted.
claims.source: Low-frequency vasomotion has been shown to be beneficial for tissue oxygenation, especially in regions where perfusion is restricted (Davis et al., 2008; Nilsson and Aalkjaer, 2003).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this benefit.

claims.claim: Vasomotion could drive paravascular clearance or intramural periarterial drainage (IPAD).
claims.source: Furthermore, it was recently reported that vasomotion could also drive paravascular clearance or intramural periarterial drainage (IPAD) (van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this function.

claims.claim: Simulation modeling suggested that vasomotion was required for efficient IPAD.
claims.source: Initially, arterial pulsation from the heart was considered to be the driving force for the IPAD; however, simulation modeling suggested that vasomotion was required for the efficient IPAD (Aldea et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this modeling result.

claims.claim: 40 Hz sensory stimulation has been proposed to be potentially beneficial for treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
claims.source: 40 Hz sensory stimulation has been proposed to be potentially beneficial for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Adaikkan et al., 2019; Iaccarino et al., 2016; Martorell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this proposal.

claims.claim: It was recently claimed that 40 Hz flickering light does not entrain gamma oscillations and suppress amyloid beta accumulation in brains of AD model mouse.
claims.source: However, it was recently claimed that the 40 Hz flickering light does not entrain gamma oscillations and suppress amyloid beta (Aβ) accumulation in the brains of the AD model mouse (Soula et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source contradicting the previous claim.

claims.claim: Flashing visual stimuli could increase the amplitude of vasomotion, which resulted in an increase in paravascular clearance rates in visual cortex of awake mice.
claims.source: In another study, it was shown that flashing visual stimuli could increase the amplitude of vasomotion, which resulted in an increase in the paravascular clearance rates in the visual cortex of awake mice (van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claims.claim: In mice with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, impaired paravascular clearance and Aβ accumulation occur.
claims.source: In mice with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, impaired paravascular clearance and Aβ accumulation occur (Charidimou et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this finding.

claims.claim: Low-frequency arteriolar oscillations could drive the drainage of soluble waste products.
claims.source: It was also suggested that low-frequency arteriolar oscillations could drive the drainage of soluble waste products (van Veluw et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this suggestion.

claims.claim: HOKR-driving oscillatory visual stimulus at 0.25 Hz is effective in producing brain-wide oscillatory vasomotion.
claims.source: In our study, we show that the HOKR-driving oscillatory visual stimulus, which is much slower (0.25 Hz) than the 40 Hz, is effective in producing a brain-wide oscillatory vasomotion.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claims.claim: Repeated presentation with spaced training protocol was effective in driving plastic vasomotion entrainment.
claims.source: In addition, repeated presentation with the spaced training protocol was effective in driving the plastic vasomotion entrainment.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claims.claim: Paravascular clearance and drainage of waste products, such as Aβ, may be enhanced with vasomotion entrainment.
claims.source: Paravascular clearance and drainage of waste products, such as Aβ, may be enhanced with vasomotion entrainment.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claims.claim: Synaptic plasticity change related to cerebellar motor learning is enhanced in parallel with vasomotion entrainment.
claims.source: We show that synaptic plasticity change related to cerebellar motor learning is enhanced in parallel with the vasomotion entrainment.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claims.claim: Vasomotion enhancement may increase meta-plasticity and provide a basis for efficient neuronal plasticity to occur.
claims.source: It is possible that vasomotion enhancement may increase the meta-plasticity and provide a basis for efficient neuronal plasticity to occur.

results.result: Spontaneous vasomotion was observed and quantified in awake mice through thinned-skull cranial windows using TexasRed fluorescence. Vasodilation events occurred periodically with an inter-event interval of 15.8 ± 4.8 s, amplitude of 10.4 ± 3.7%, and half-width duration of 1.6 ± 0.4 s. Vessel diameter measurements (45.7 ± 9.6 µm) indicated observation of pial arteries or arterioles.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C44 provide converging evidence from direct observations (C36, C39), validated measurement methods (C40, C42), and quantitative characterization (C43, C44) of spontaneous vasomotion. The measurements are internally consistent and the vessel type inference (C41) is reasonable based on diameter data.

results.result: Endogenous autofluorescence from brain parenchyma can be used to quantify vasomotion through the 'shadow' imaging principle. Autofluorescence (excited at ~430 nm, emission ~540 nm) is absent from blood vessels, and autofluorescence dynamics mirror TexasRed fluorescence dynamics in blood vessels, allowing vasomotion quantification through intact skull.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C48-C51 establish the methodological principle with direct observations showing spatial separation (C49) and temporal correlation (C50) between autofluorescence and TexasRed signals. Claims C46-C47 validate the method's applicability through intact skull, addressing a key technical challenge.

results.result: Visual stimulation with horizontally oscillating vertical stripes (0.25 Hz) induces frequency-locked vasomotion that becomes entrained with repeated training. This entrainment progresses from Novice (no fixed frequency) to Trained (clear 0.25 Hz peak) to Expert (visible oscillations in raw traces), and occurs globally across cortex and cerebellum, not just in visual areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5-C6, C29-C30, C57-C58, C61-C67 provide comprehensive evidence for plastic vasomotion entrainment. The progression from Novice to Expert is well-documented with spectral analysis (C57-C58, C61), temporal dynamics (C62-C63), and spatial distribution data (C64-C67) showing global rather than local effects.

results.result: Visually induced vasomotion adapts to a wide range of stimulation parameters. Vasomotion can lock to temporal frequencies from 0.15-0.50 Hz, spatial amplitudes from 4-25°, and various spatial cycles of stripe patterns, with no significant differences in peak ratio across these parameter ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C83-C89 demonstrate parameter flexibility through systematic variation experiments. Statistical analysis (C84) confirms no significant differences across temporal frequencies, and similar robustness is shown for amplitude (C87-C88) and spatial cycle (C89) variations, supporting the broad adaptability claim.

results.result: There is a strong correlation between HOKR performance gain and vasomotion entrainment magnitude in the cerebellar flocculus. Average HOKR relative gains correlated strongly with average PR0.25 values across training sessions (C101), and a moderate correlation was found between day 5 HOKR performance and day 1 vasomotion levels (C103), suggesting parallel plasticity of vasomotion and neuronal circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C33, C99-C105 establish correlations between behavioral and vascular measures. The strong population-level correlation (C101) is supported by quantitative data from 15 mice across 10 tests. The moderate individual-level correlation (C103) and large variance (C102) are appropriately acknowledged, supporting the interpretation of parallel plasticity (C105).

results.result: Direct YFP fluorescence (dYFP) from astrocyte-expressed YCnano50 can be used to assess vasomotion dynamics in deep brain regions via fiber photometry. TexasRed and dYFP signals fluctuated at 0.25 Hz with nearly opposite phase (184.4° ± 17.6°), demonstrating vasomotion in the cerebellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 validate the dYFP shadow imaging method with quantitative phase analysis showing near-perfect inversion. Claim C74 extends vasomotion detection to deep cerebellar regions. However, C77 notes this approach failed for HOKR learning studies, limiting its broader applicability.

results.result: Autofluorescence signals measured by fiber photometry show a phase shift (246.9° ± 49.9°) relative to TexasRed, likely due to combined effects of shadow imaging and metabolite concentration fluctuations. Despite this phase shift, PR0.25 of autofluorescence strongly correlates with TexasRed PR0.25 and reflects vasomotion amplitude locked to visual stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 acknowledge a methodological complexity (phase shift) while demonstrating that the metric (PR0.25) remains valid. The strong correlation (C81) between autofluorescence and TexasRed PR0.25 supports using autofluorescence for quantifying vasomotion amplitude despite the phase shift. The proposed explanation (C79) is speculative but reasonable.

results.result: Vasomotion is not a direct consequence of eye movements. Eye movements tracked visual stimulation with virtually no phase shift (C90), but vasomotion phase in the flocculus varied between animals (0° or 180°, C91). Under anesthesia, neither eye movement nor vasomotion occurred (C93), and no correlation was found between eye movement amplitude and vasomotion amplitude within sessions (C95-C96).
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 provide multiple lines of evidence ruling out eye movement as the direct cause of vasomotion. Control experiments (C93-C94) eliminate artifacts, and the lack of correlation between eye movement and vasomotion amplitudes (C95-C96) within sessions is particularly compelling. The variable phase relationship (C91) further supports independence.

results.result: Vasomotion can be quantified in non-transgenic wild-type mice using either wide-field macro-zoom microscopy or deep-brain fiber photometry methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 are directly supported by the experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript. Both methods are validated with autofluorescence measurements in wild-type mice, avoiding the need for transgenic animals. This is a significant methodological advance.

results.result: Repeated trials of visual stimulus presentations result in plastic entrainment of vasomotion, with the entrainment becoming perfectly frequency-locked to presented stimuli with repeated training.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C29, C138 describe the core plasticity phenomenon. The progression from non-entrained to entrained states is well-documented through spectral analysis and temporal dynamics data. The term 'perfectly frequency-locked' (C29) may be slightly overstated given the variability noted in C62-C63, but the overall plasticity is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Plasticity of vasomotion and neuronal circuits occur in parallel, with synaptic plasticity related to cerebellar motor learning enhanced alongside vasomotion entrainment.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C34, C105, C140 propose parallel plasticity based on correlations between HOKR performance and vasomotion. While the correlations are demonstrated (C101, C103), the causal relationship and mechanistic basis remain unclear. The large variance (C102) and moderate individual-level correlation (C103) suggest the relationship is complex. Additional experiments would be needed to establish whether these are truly parallel processes or if one drives the other.

results.result: Efficient energy delivery by entrained vasomotion may contribute to meeting energy demand for neuronal activity and circuit reorganization, potentially enhancing meta-plasticity and supporting long-term plastic changes in the brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C104, C139, C141, C145 propose functional significance of vasomotion entrainment but are largely speculative. While the correlation data (C101, C103) are consistent with this interpretation, no direct measurements of energy delivery, metabolic demand, or meta-plasticity are provided. These remain hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Spontaneous vasomotion in awake mice shows oscillatory fluctuations at low frequencies (0.1-0.5 Hz) that are less periodic than previously reported, possibly due to interruptions from spontaneous behaviors causing functional hyperemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 describe characteristics of spontaneous vasomotion with appropriate caveats. The observation of variable frequency (C53) and proposed explanation involving behavioral interruptions (C54) is reasonable given the awake preparation. This contrasts with more periodic vasomotion reported in other preparations, which is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Stress induced by tail vein injection may interfere with HOKR learning acquisition but does not interfere with generation of visually induced vasomotion or maintenance of already acquired HOKR learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C113 describe an important methodological observation. The differential effects on learning acquisition versus maintenance/vasomotion generation are clearly demonstrated and led to the development of the autofluorescence method. This is well-supported by the experimental observations.

results.result: The initial drive for visually induced vasomotion likely comes from neuronal activity in the visual system via neurovascular coupling, but the global entrainment mechanism remains unclear and could involve either central control through autonomic projections or enhanced local neurovascular and vascular-to-vascular coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 propose mechanisms for vasomotion induction and global entrainment but are largely speculative. While the initial neurovascular coupling trigger (C106-C107) is well-supported by prior literature, the mechanisms for global entrainment (C108-C110) are hypothetical. The manuscript does not provide direct evidence to distinguish between the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: The phase shift observed in autofluorescence signals may reflect temporal lag in metabolite concentration changes (NADH, NADPH, FAD) relative to blood flow changes, with glucose and oxygen delivery varying between vasodilation and vasoconstriction phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112, C79 propose a mechanistic explanation for the observed phase shift in autofluorescence. While physiologically plausible, this remains speculative without direct measurements of metabolite concentrations or identification of the autofluorescent species. The explanation is reasonable but unproven.

results.result: Imaging through intact skull coated with transparent resin allows visualization of blood vessels without invasive procedures that could perturb vasomotion, though with reduced resolution compared to thinned-skull preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C45-C46 describe methodological considerations and solutions. The concern about perturbation from invasive procedures (C37, C45) is well-founded and cited. The intact skull method (C38, C46) successfully addresses this concern while acknowledging the trade-off in image quality. This is a practical methodological contribution.

results.result: The mechanisms underlying visually induced vasomotion are unclear and could involve spontaneous vasomotion mechanisms (SMC coordination, pericyte control), functional hyperemia mechanisms (neurovascular coupling), or systemic factors (blood pressure, CO2), with multiple cellular players (SMCs, pericytes, astrocytes, neurons) potentially involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C123 provide a comprehensive discussion of potential mechanisms, appropriately acknowledging uncertainty (C114) while reviewing established knowledge from the literature. This represents a fair assessment of the current state of understanding rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Previous studies showed that visual stimulation induces functional hyperemia and that periodic visual stimuli can induce vasomotion at matching frequencies, but this was reported to be restricted to the visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126, C28 accurately summarize prior work with appropriate citations. This provides important context for the novelty of the current findings showing global rather than local vasomotion entrainment. The citations appear accurate based on the references provided.

results.result: Vasomotion has been shown to be beneficial for blood flow efficiency, tissue oxygenation, and paravascular clearance/waste drainage, with mathematical modeling supporting these functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131, C21-C22 accurately summarize established findings from the literature with appropriate citations. This provides important functional context for why vasomotion entrainment might be significant, though these are not new findings from the current study.

results.result: The study's findings on low-frequency (0.25 Hz) vasomotion entrainment may have implications for Alzheimer's disease treatment, as vasomotion can enhance paravascular clearance of waste products like Aβ, though this remains speculative and requires validation in AD models.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137, C139, C146 discuss potential therapeutic implications but are highly speculative. While the connection to paravascular clearance is supported by prior literature (C134-C136), the therapeutic potential for AD (C139) is hypothetical. The manuscript appropriately notes that evidence in AD models would be required (implied in discussion), but this remains an untested hypothesis.

results.result: Horizontally oscillating visual stimuli induce HOKR, with eye movement amplitude increasing through repeated training via neuronal circuit plasticity in the cerebellar flocculus.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C31-C32, C55-C56, C97-C98 accurately describe established knowledge about HOKR with appropriate citations. This provides essential background for understanding the experimental paradigm used in the study. The citations to prior work appear accurate.

results.result: Neuron-astrocyte signaling pathways in the cerebellum are essential for HOKR learning, with late offline learning dependent on astrocyte phagocytosis activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 accurately summarize recent findings on the cellular mechanisms of HOKR learning with appropriate citations. This provides important context for interpreting the vasomotion-HOKR correlation findings, suggesting potential roles for astrocytes in coordinating vascular and neuronal plasticity.

results.result: Energy consumption in the brain is super-efficient compared to computers, with energy delivered via blood vessels. Spontaneous vasomotion (~0.1 Hz) is distinct from heartbeat pulsation (~10 Hz) and was first described in bat wing veins.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 provide accurate background information with appropriate citations. The distinction between vasomotion and heartbeat pulsation (C19-C20) is important for understanding the phenomenon studied. These represent established knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Vasomotion can be affected by neurovascular coupling mechanisms, where neuronal firing triggers release of vasodilator signals from neurons/astrocytes, leading to blood vessel dilation through SMC and pericyte relaxation (functional hyperemia), which underlies fMRI signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 accurately describe established neurovascular coupling mechanisms with appropriate citations. This provides essential background for understanding how visual stimulation could affect vasomotion. The connection to fMRI (C27) is well-established.

results.result: Blood vessels in the brain can change their diameter through the actions of SMCs and pericytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 states basic established knowledge about vascular control mechanisms with appropriate citations. This is fundamental background information for the study.

results.result: C57BL/6NJcl male mice (2-4 months old) were used to reduce variance of HOKR performance among animals.
results.evaluation: Claim C147 describes the experimental subjects with appropriate justification and citation. This is a reasonable methodological choice for reducing variability in behavioral experiments.

results.result: The authors developed and validated a novel method using endogenous autofluorescence to quantify vasomotion by measuring the vessel 'shadow' in wild-type mice. This method works with both wide-field macro-zoom microscopy and deep-brain fiber photometry, and the autofluorescence signals correlate strongly with direct vessel diameter measurements using TexasRed fluorescence.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly acknowledge this methodological contribution. Reviewer 1 states the method 'allows vasomotion to be easily quantified' and Reviewer 3 describes it as 'a simple and useful method for tracking vasomotion in awake mice through an intact skull.' The reviewers note the validation showing autofluorescence 'correlates well with the intensity profile of fluorescently-labelled single vessels' without raising concerns about the approach.

results.result: Oscillating visual stimuli at 0.25 Hz induce vasomotion that becomes frequency-locked and phase-synchronized across the entire cortical surface and cerebellum, not just in the visual cortex. This global entrainment develops with repeated training and represents plastic enhancement of vasomotion.
results.evaluation: All reviewers highlight this as a central finding. The editor notes 'plastic enhancement in the vasomotion response' as an 'important result,' Reviewer 1 emphasizes the authors 'demonstrate the ability to entrain vasomotion across multiple brain areas,' and Reviewer 3 specifically mentions 'the nearly brain-wide synchronization of cerebral blood flow oscillations to visual stimuli' as an 'interesting observation.' No concerns are raised about this claim.

results.result: Visually induced vasomotion adapts to a wide range of stimulation parameters (temporal frequency 0.15-0.50 Hz, amplitude 4-25°, spatial cycles) and shows plastic entrainment that increases with repeated training sessions, progressing from Novice to Trained to Expert states.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding without critique. Reviewer 1 notes 'the amplitude spectrum of the detected vasomotion frequency increases with repeated training sessions' and Reviewer 3 states 'repeated trials led to plastic entrainment.' The editor describes the evidence as 'solid' and notes the effect occurs 'using a wide range of external visual stimulation paradigms.'

results.result: There is a strong correlation between HOKR performance gain and vasomotion entrainment magnitude in the cerebellar flocculus, suggesting that plasticity of vasomotion and neuronal circuits occur in parallel and that vasomotion may contribute to motor learning consolidation.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this correlation as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'attempt to demonstrate some functional benefit of vasomotion entraining as HOKR performance improves' and notes 'HOKR task performance correlates well with vascular oscillation amplitudes.' Reviewer 3 mentions 'a strong correlation with CBF entrainment magnitude in the cerebellar flocculus' and that 'parallel plasticity in CBF and neuronal circuits is occurring.' No concerns are raised about the correlation analysis.

results.result: Spontaneous vasomotion was observed in awake, unanesthetized mice through both thinned-skull and intact skull preparations, showing periodic vasodilation events with characteristic temporal dynamics (inter-event interval ~15.8 s) and low-frequency oscillations (0.1-0.5 Hz).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these observations without critique. Reviewer 1 notes 'spontaneous vasomotion could be detected in individual vessels of their wild-type mice through either a thinned cranial window or intact skull preparation.' The characterization of spontaneous vasomotion serves as baseline for the induced vasomotion experiments that reviewers find compelling.

results.result: Control experiments demonstrate that the observed vasomotion signals are not artifacts of eye movement or direct light contamination from the visual stimulus screen. Eye movement and vasomotion show different phase relationships, and no correlation exists between eye movement amplitude and vasomotion amplitude within single sessions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly acknowledges 'the authors include some control experiments to rule out fluorescence fluctuations being due to artifacts of eye movement or screen luminance.' Reviewer 3 states 'the work controls for artefacts in their primary measurements' and lists 'light contamination and eye movements' as controlled variables, finding 'no influence of these variables.'

results.result: The authors propose that efficient energy delivery by entrained vasomotion may support increased coordinated neuronal activity and neuronal circuit reorganization, with vasomotion plasticity potentially enhancing meta-plasticity and interacting with neuronal circuit plasticity.
results.evaluation: While these are interpretive claims, reviewers accept them without challenge. The editor notes the findings are 'relevant for scientists and clinicians interested in the regulation of blood flow in the brain,' implicitly accepting the functional significance. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'propose that entrained vasomotion contributes to meeting the increased energy demand' without expressing skepticism about this interpretation.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the autofluorescence method for measuring vasomotion (C2, C48-C51). OpenEval emphasizes methodological validation with spatial/temporal separation, while peer reviewers highlight practical utility ('easily quantified', 'simple and useful method'). Peer review also includes validation claims C76, C81, C82 that OpenEval addresses separately in R7.

Both strongly support vasomotion entrainment findings (C1, C5-C6, C29-C30, C65-C67). OpenEval provides detailed spectral and spatial analysis, while peer reviewers emphasize the 'nearly brain-wide synchronization' and describe evidence as 'solid'. Both note the global rather than local nature of the effect.

Both support parameter flexibility claims (C7, C83-C89). OpenEval focuses on systematic variation experiments showing robustness across temporal frequencies, amplitude, and spatial cycles. Peer reviewers acknowledge the effect occurs 'using a wide range of external visual stimulation paradigms' and note 'repeated trials led to plastic entrainment.'

Strong agreement on HOKR-vasomotion correlation (C12, C33, C99-C105). Both acknowledge population-level correlation (C101) and moderate individual-level correlation (C103). OpenEval notes large variance and parallel plasticity interpretation; peer reviewers accept correlation without critique and note 'parallel plasticity in CBF and neuronal circuits is occurring.'

Strong agreement on control experiments ruling out eye movement artifacts (C90, C93-C96). OpenEval emphasizes multiple lines of evidence including lack of correlation and variable phase relationships. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge these controls and find 'no influence of these variables.'

Both support spontaneous vasomotion observations (C36, C39, C43-C44). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative characterization and vessel type inference. Peer reviewers acknowledge these observations as baseline for induced vasomotion experiments. Peer review also includes C52-C53 on variable frequency that OpenEval addresses in R13.

Both support the methodological advance of using autofluorescence in wild-type mice (C3-C4). OpenEval emphasizes avoiding transgenic animals as significant advance. Peer review includes these claims within broader methodological validation (R1) that also covers C48-C51, C76, C81-C82.

Both support the validity of autofluorescence measurements despite phase shift (C78-C82). OpenEval acknowledges methodological complexity while demonstrating strong correlation (C81) validates the metric. Peer reviewers include C81-C82 in their overall acceptance of the method without expressing concerns about the phase shift.

Divergence in certainty about parallel plasticity interpretation (C13, C34, C105, C140). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting correlations don't establish causality and mechanistic basis remains unclear. Peer reviewers SUPPORT these interpretive claims, accepting the parallel plasticity framework without expressing skepticism about causal relationships.

Divergence on functional significance claims (C14, C104, C139, C141, C145). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, calling these 'largely speculative' without direct metabolic measurements. Peer reviewers SUPPORT, accepting the functional interpretation that 'entrained vasomotion contributes to meeting increased energy demand' without challenge.

Both address mechanistic claims about vasomotion induction (C106-C107). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting neurovascular coupling trigger is well-supported but global entrainment mechanisms are hypothetical. Peer reviewers include these in accepted functional interpretation without distinguishing supported from speculative elements.

Both support characterization of spontaneous vasomotion (C52-C53). OpenEval notes variable frequency with appropriate caveats and reasonable explanation involving behavioral interruptions. Peer reviewers acknowledge these observations as part of baseline characterization without critique.

Both support core plasticity phenomenon (C8, C29). OpenEval notes progression from non-entrained to entrained states is well-documented, though 'perfectly frequency-locked' may be slightly overstated. Peer reviewers emphasize this as central finding without concerns about terminology.
